identified_problems.explanation: The cited January statement concerned regret about not using the National Guard to seize election equipment after the 2020 election; it was not a direct threat to deploy troops to 2026 polling places.

frozen_original.title: Trump Threatens to Deploy National Guard to 2026 Midterm Polling Places
frozen_original.synopsis: In a January 7, 2026 New York Times interview, Trump expressed regret that he had not directed the National Guard to seize voting machines after the 2020 election, signaling his intent to use military force around the 2026 midterms. Trump had already deployed the National Guard to at least four Democratic-led cities against the will of their governors in 2025, with courts issuing multiple injunctions. A February 2026 PBS News report revealed a 17-page draft executive order circulating among Trump allies that would declare a national emergency to take federal control over midterm elections, require hand-counting of ballots, and force voters to re-register with proof of citizenship. Trump publicly threatened on Truth Social: 'There will be Voter I.D. for the Midterm Elections, whether approved by Congress or not!' Legal experts said any troop deployment to polls would violate multiple federal statutes.

frozen_original.title: Trump Demands Loyalty Oath from Senior Federal Employees
frozen_original.synopsis: In mid-February 2025, the Trump administration began requiring senior career federal employees to sign personal loyalty statements pledging fidelity to the president and his agenda as a condition of continued employment. The demands went beyond the constitutional oath to defend the Constitution, requiring personal loyalty to Trump specifically. Several senior officials refused and were placed on administrative leave pending termination. Good-government groups noted that personal loyalty oaths to a leader rather than to the Constitution are a hallmark of authoritarian governments. The American Bar Association condemned the practice as incompatible with the rule of law and the constitutional design of the federal civil service.

proposal.original_claim_summary: DOGE Fires 1,300 Department of Education Employees
proposal.original_synopsis: In March 2025, the Department of Government Efficiency directed the termination of approximately 1,300 Department of Education employees — roughly half the department's total workforce — through a combination of mass firings and forced buyouts. Among those eliminated were staff overseeing Title I funding for low-income schools, special education enforcement under IDEA, student loan servicing oversight, and the Office for Civil Rights which investigated discrimination at schools. Education Secretary Linda McMahon described the firings as the first step toward eliminating the department entirely. States reported losing their primary federal contacts for education compliance. Civil rights complaints filed by students and parents began piling up with no staff to process them. Teachers unions called the action a deliberate sabotage of public education infrastructure.

proposal.original_claim_summary: FBI under Patel begins monitoring mosques and Muslim community organizations
proposal.original_synopsis: Under Kash Patel's leadership, the FBI reinstituted surveillance programs targeting mosques and Muslim community organizations, reviving religious profiling and First Amendment violations. The program assigned FBI agents to regularly monitor sermons, track attendees, and develop informants inside Muslim communities across the United States. The move echoed post-9/11 surveillance abuses and was condemned by Muslim civil rights organizations as a return to discriminatory religious profiling that had previously been found to produce no actionable intelligence.
